reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it is presented as a beginner Tagalog guide and screen-recorded walkthrough of a game's site, trailers, white paper, and gameplay rather than a transaction process. Play-to-earn features such as collections, breeding, rare traits, and rewards are described as reported game mechanics, without established earnings, costs, or outcomes. Although the speaker discusses backers and directs viewers to game and social destinations, the speaker identifies backers as only one research factor, advises viewers to do their own research, and leaves the displayed partner and team information unverified.

citations.quote: This Tagalog guide covers everything you need to know as a beginner
Full gameplay demo of SolChicks
today, we'll be doing another game review
buy and sell, soul chicks with the community, great collections and earn rewards
Breed adorable Soul Chicks, unlock sell soulchecks with the community create collections or and earn rewards

opening.argument: Judge the invitation and the reward claim together. The site presents the game as play-to-earn and offers a game demo and community links; the speaker then describes creating collections to earn rewards and tells viewers that earnings from these games could build funds for other projects. He also directs viewers to links in the description. That is more than an account of game mechanics: it gives viewers a route toward participation while making earnings the reason to take it. The video does not establish what a player must spend, what rewards are worth, or whether those earnings can be realized. Those omissions matter when the participation pitch rests on earning.

citations.quote: sell soulchecks with the community create collections or and earn rewards
you could stack up your funds you know you could earn in these games
Link will be in the description of the video, Discord, Twitter, and their Telegram link will also be in the description.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense calls this a beginner walkthrough, but a walkthrough can also direct a viewer toward an earning opportunity. Its own cited mechanics include buying, selling, and earning rewards. Nor does calling backers one research factor resolve the concern: the speaker goes on to describe earning, building funds, and reinvesting. The issue is not whether he quotes a guaranteed return; it is whether the game demonstration makes an unsubstantiated earning path attractive enough to pursue.

citations.quote: buy and sell, soul chicks with the community, great collections and earn rewards
you could also reinvest your earnings in other projects

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The cited material does not promise easy or assured income. The page's play-to-earn description and the speaker's discussion of collections identify game features, while his phrasing says viewers could earn, not that they will. He explicitly urges research and warns that the space contains scammers. The absence of verified earnings is a reason to avoid treating the claims as established, but it does not itself establish a deceptive reward scheme.

citations.quote: you could earn in these games
you just have to do your own research and make sure that what you're getting into is the right one
there are also a lot of scammers there's a lot of rug pullers

opening.argument: Look at how the credibility signals accumulate around the earning claim. The speaker cites large Telegram and Discord audiences, shows a page headed by partner logos, and reads a claim that the team has a proven track record. He then describes the project as a better starting point after recounting his own experience of being rugged. Alongside the play-to-earn pitch, that combination asks viewers to take apparent popularity, affiliations, and team claims as reassurance. None of those displayed claims verifies that a player can earn usable rewards or avoid loss. A careful judge should treat the repeated reassurance as part of the solicitation, not as independent proof of safety.

citations.quote: Salt Chicks already has a more than 180k members in their Telegram and in their Discord. They already have more than 170k members.
Fully integrated team with a proven track record of Building successful blockchain projects
I mean I myself have been rugged a with the previous games that I tried before so with projects like this at least you could start off on the right foot

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense says the backer and team information remains unverified. That is precisely why its persuasive use matters: the speaker does not merely display it, but says backers merit consideration and describes their support as evidence a project had to defend its prospects. The warning to research limits the pitch, yet it does not verify the community counts, affiliations, or team claims used to make this earning-oriented project seem safer.

for them to back up a project, guys, it's like that project has to pitch and defend themselves on what they can do for the project to be successful

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The argument correctly notes that promotional claims are not independent verification, but supplies no evidence that those claims are false or that rewards cannot be earned. The speaker expressly says backers should not be the decision-making criterion, calls for viewers' own research, and discusses the risk of scams and rug pulls. Reading unverified claims skeptically is warranted; converting them into evidence of deception is not.

opening.argument: The review format should not obscure what the speaker asks viewers to do. He supplies a route to the game's site and social channels, tells viewers they can click through, and frames those links as a way to avoid phishing sites. During the walkthrough he calls the game one of the best, discusses its buy-and-sell and reward features, and strongly suggests that newcomers start with projects he considers better prepared. The result functions as promotion of participation in an earning-oriented NFT game, even though it contains gameplay footage and research cautions. The judge should weigh the directional recommendation and click-through path, not just the video's stated educational purpose.

This is one of the best. That's an easy pick.
buy and sell, soul chicks with the community, great collections and earn rewards
I would strongly suggest that you start off with Triple A projects.

rebuttal.rebuttal: A beginner guide and gameplay demo can still be promotional. The defense emphasizes that there is no transaction process on screen, but the speaker gives viewers a path to the project and recommends where newcomers should start. Saying that the links support research does not erase the affirmative recommendation, especially when he ties participation in these games to the possibility of earning and reinvesting.

you could earn in these games and then i'm not saying that you just have to focus on this one you could also reinvest your earnings in other projects

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Promotion is not, by itself, a scam mechanism. The speaker presents a game review, examines gameplay and the project's site, and explicitly treats backers as only one consideration rather than a basis for a decision. His research and scam warnings also qualify the recommendation. The prosecution identifies enthusiasm and links, but not a guaranteed reward, a false claim, or a demonstrated deceptive participation flow.
